title: The Salt Road
logline: A salt-counter discovers her annual tally has been altered and must decide whether a true complaint is worth the town's peace.
thematic_question: What does it cost to hold a truth the town has agreed not to want?

characters.name: Maren
characters.want: to prove the tally was altered before the spring hearing
characters.need: to accept that being believed is not the same as being safe
characters.wound: Her mother counted salt for forty years and was never once believed.
characters.secret: She has kept a private tally for eleven years.
characters.voice: Short declaratives; repeats the other person's words back as a question.

knowledge.fact: The tithe was short by two sacks when she counted it
Complaints are heard in the spring

characters.name: Dov
characters.want: to be seen as a fair man by the upper town
characters.need: to admit fairness has never cost him anything
characters.wound: He was believed once when he was wrong, and it was profitable.
characters.voice: Repeats the official phrasing of the upper town as if it were his own.

knowledge.fact: The clerk announced the shortfall in public

characters.name: The clerk
characters.need: to be named out loud rather than described by his office
characters.voice: Administrative register; never uses a first person plural.

knowledge.fact: The ledger page is not a public page

locations.name: The tithe barn
locations.description: Where the salt is counted and where the neighbours gather.
locations.constraints: One door; the road is visible from it.

locations.name: The clerk's office
locations.description: Cold, clean, smells of floor polish.

locations.name: The tide market
locations.description: A market that opens only at low tide and is absent from this draft section.

factions.name: The upper town
factions.goal: Convert the tithe into a permanent administrative right.
factions.resources: The bell, the ledger, the hearing calendar.

factions.name: The salt-counting houses
factions.goal: Keep the annual count under local authority.

rules.statement: The tithe is counted twice: once by the household, once by the clerk.
rules.cost: The clerk's count is the only count entered in the record.
rules.limits: A household may formally complain, but only in spring.

rules.statement: Each house keeps its own tally in a private ledger.
rules.cost: A private tally cannot be entered as evidence.
rules.limits: Only the counter may read it aloud.

items.name: The clerk's ledger
items.state: held against his chest when first described
items.significance: The only record the town treats as true.

items.name: Maren's private tally
items.state: eleven years of entries, in her hand

timeline.event: Maren counts the tithe and finds it short by two sacks.
The clerk announces the shortfall in front of the neighbours.
Maren asks to see the ledger page and is refused.
Three neighbours gather in the barn and leave without a decision.

threads.question: Will Maren be believed about the missing sacks?
Will Dov choose the upper town or the barn?
What does the bell's exact hour mean to the town?
threads.payoff: It marks the administrative day, not a warning.

sources.claim: Salt was taxed by weight in household lots rather than by value.
sources.source: internal research note; verify against a regional customs history before publication

sources.claim: The upper town bell was rung by a clerk rather than a sexton.
sources.notes: Keep it framed as fiction; never presented as documented history.

glossary.meaning: The annual salt levy counted in household lots.
The administrative quarter that holds the record.

notes.usage: Fixture for the continuity operation and the self-test. Deliberately contains one unused location and two open threads so the audit reports real findings.
